Chief Executive’s Monthly Management Report – 31st October 2025 
 
 
 
A Chara, 
 
I enclose the above report for your statutory consideration, this report has also been prepared under Section 136 
& 138 of the Local Government Act, 2001. The attached report is the Chief Executive’s Monthly Management 
Report for October 2025, detailing activities, updates, and progress across various departments of Louth County 
Council.  
 
Key achievements and actions under various directorates from the Chief Executive Report for October 2025: 
 
1. Finance and System Support Directorate 
• 
Expenditure to date: €140.88M (77% of budget spent). 
• 
Income to date: €134.40M (73% invoiced). 
• 
Debtors closing balance: €55.70M. 
• 
Prepare 2025 - Budget 2026 meeting scheduled for 17th November 2025. 
• 
We continue to  target  phishing, and spam e-mail, in October 13.81% of inbound e-mails were identified 
as potentially harmful.

15,800 web pages where unique views in October. 
 
2. Economic Delivery Directorate

Dominican Church was transformed and hosted the Cottage Market Traders, 
• 
Boyne Valley Flavours launched a new website and hosted workshops. 
• 
Purple Flag assessment visit showcased Drogheda’s night-time economy. 
• 
National Women’s Enterprise Day celebrated with 60 female entrepreneurs. 
• 
Louth Business Awards recognized SafeShel as Best New Start-Up. 
• 
For September , 92 planning applications received, 77 valid, 40 FOI queries issued and 21 Pre-Planning 
requests. 
 
3. Operations & Environment Delivery Directorate 
• 
Extensive road repairs, drainage remediation, and illegal dumping cleanups across municipal districts. 
• 
Waste enforcement: 170 water warning issues issued, 27 complaints investigated, 14 fixed payment 
notices issued. 
• 
Household Hazardous Waste Collection Day successfully hosted. 
• 
CCTV cameras operational at 5 sites, deterring illegal dumping, with multiagency checkpoints. 
• 
Climate Action Week events included beach cleanups and awareness campaigns. 
• 
24 Dogs went through the dog pound and 454 dog licences sold. 
• 
The Fire service successfully achieved the  NSAI ISO 45001 Health and Safety surveillance audit. 
• 
Call Out of the fire service – 137 incidents in October, 14 of these on the evening of 31st October. 
 
4. HR, Corporate & Community Delivery Directorate 
• 
During the month of October 2025 Customer Services dealt with 16,839 queries inclusive of 8,492 calls, 
1,177 e-mails and 7170 counter queries. 9928 (59%) of queries received were dealt with at first point of 
contact. 
• 
The Presidential Election took place on Friday the 24th October 2025. A large amount of work was 
completed within the Franchise Section in the weeks running up to the election, with a consistently high 
rate of applications being received via www.checktheregister.ie. The total electorate for Presidential

Cyber Security 
The ICT Department delivers regular cybersecurity training to all staff across the organisation. The October 
training focused on Cyber Security Month and featured a message from the Louth County Council Chief 
Executive, emphasising the importance of promptly reporting any suspected cybersecurity incidents. The session 
also addressed social engineering tactics commonly used by cybercriminals. Staff were reminded to pause and 
think before responding to emails or text messages that create a sense of urgency, and to always verify the 
legitimacy of such messages with the IT Team before taking any action.

Night Curation Scheme — Over the Top 
Wrestling at The Barbican 
Local event organiser Keith Dunne (wrestling stage 
name Calum Black) became the latest participant in 
the Night Curation Scheme, which supports via 
funding, mentoring, and data sharing.  Working with 
Over the Top Wrestling (OTT), Keith brought a high-
quality family event to The Barbican and town centre 
on Saturday, 11th October (7–9.30pm), following an 
earlier trial at a local GAA club.  The show sold 400+ 
tickets, with 22% of sales outside Louth, showing 
strong regional draw and potential to grow into a 
recurring 
feature. 
 The 
production 
included 
professional lighting, sound, and merchandise, 
transforming the Barbican into a purpose-built arena 
for one night.  OTT included contenders from 
Ireland, the US, France, Italy and Spain, raising 
Drogheda’s profile on the independent wrestling 
circuit.   
 
Plans are now in place for a return in early 2026, 
supported through the Night-Time Economy Adviser 
to develop a regular series of town-centre events. 
 
Safe Gigs Ireland Consultation  
The Drogheda Purple Flag Working Group has 
partnered with Safe Gigs Ireland to provide tailored 
safeguarding consultations for local night operators 
under the Purple Flag Charter.  The first consultation 
sessions took place on Tuesday, 21st October, 
engaging three pubs, one restaurant, and a 
grassroots music venue.  Each participant receives 
individual guidance to develop or enhance a written 
safeguarding protocol and staff training plan suited 
to their venue’s scale and activity.  The approach 
builds a proactive safety culture, focusing on 
prevention, awareness, and staff confidence rather 
than reactive measures.  While primarily aimed at 
venues and event organisers, future sessions will 
extend to retail, transport and other late operators, 
ensuring Drogheda’s night-time sector moves 
forward together under a shared standard of care.

Purple Flag Assessment Visit 
On Saturday, 25th October, Drogheda welcomed two 
Purple Flag assessors as part of its bid to retain 
Purple Flag status, recognising excellence in 
evening and night-time management.  Twelve 
partner organisations — including An Garda 
Síochána, Safe Gigs Ireland, Louth County Council, 
Droichead Arts Centre, Love Drogheda BID, 
Drogheda & District Chamber, and local event 
organisers — presented updates on a year of 
collaboration and delivery.   
 
The assessors then toured the town during the Lú 
Festival of Lights, seeing Drogheda at its best: opera 
performances, upgraded Garda CCTV, late-night 
cafés, new festival-linked events, Highlanes Gallery 
open late, and a thriving food and nightlife offer 
including D’Vine Bistro and Tapas.  The tour 
continued until the early hours of the morning to 
observe the different phases of the night-time 
economy.  The visit showcased strong local 
partnership, a visible culture of care, and the town’s 
commitment to arts and creativity.  Early feedback 
was positive, noting Drogheda’s clear strategy, civic 
pride, and growing identity as Ireland’s east coast 
alternative.

Young people from Comhairle na nÓg took part in a 
special consultation event held in the Market house in 
Dunleer. Twenty six young people participated in the 
consultation and represented all three Municipal 
Districts in Louth. 
 
The format of the consultation was to use non formal 
education methods to create an environment for the 
young people to share their ideas on the play and 
recreation needs for their communities as part of the 
Council’s consultation process for the development of 
Play Recreation and Sports Strategies. This included 
warm up games, clarifications on the meaning of play, 
recreation and an overview of the consultation 
process.  
 
The young people then got to address the key 
questions and give feedback and discussion on their 
responses. This was completed in an open World Café 
style and used a placemat and Post Its to gather 
responses. 
The event was facilitated by the Youth Work teams of 
Dundalk Youth Centre, Boomerang Young Peoples 
Centre and Mid Louth Youth Service.  The feedback 
was then compiled and the young people decided on 
the recommendations to be included in this report. 
 
Recommendations 
 
The importance of Play Recreation and Sport 
 
1. Increase Opportunities for Social Interaction 
Since many responses mention making friends, 
meeting new people and building confidence, 
programmes 
should 
prioritise 
group-based 
recreational activities that encourage teamwork, 
communication and friendship-building. 
 
2. Focus on Wellbeing and Stress Relief 
Young people repeatedly highlighted stress reduction, 
relaxation and improving mental health. This shows a 
need for spaces and activities that promote calmness 
and emotional wellbeing. 
 
3. Support Skill-Building and Personal Growth 
Feedback such as learning new skills, building self-
confidence and developing personal interests in 
recreational activities that build life and social skills. 
 
Barriers to getting involved in Play Recreation and 
Sport 
 
1. Social and Emotional Barriers 
Young people identified several social barriers to 
participation 
in 
play 
and 
recreation, 
including 
experiences of bullying, judgment, fear of making 
mistakes, peer pressure, embarrassment, negative 
public perceptions and popular stereotypes that 
portray teenagers as disinterested or unmotivated. 
 
2. Mental Health, Wellbeing, Time, and Pressure 
Young people highlighted personal barriers such as 
anxiety, mental health challenges, negative home 
environments and low confidence or fear of 
participation. It was noted that school-related stress 
and time pressures, along with extracurricular 
activities becoming overly serious or competitive, can 
limit their participation in play and recreation. 
 
3. Practical and Structural Barriers 
Young people reported structural barriers, including a 
lack of services and suitable facilities, limited access 
to plays or theatre, rural isolation, lack of transport and 
financial constraints affecting affordability.  
 
In addition, there are a lot of facilities that could be put 
to better use for young people’s recreation. 
 
New Play Recreation and Sports Ideas 
 
1.  Create More Outdoor Social and Sport Spaces 
There was repeated reference to parks, skate parks, 
football 
pitches, 
beach 
seats 
and 
all-season 
recreational sports and another Aura. 
 
2. Develop Multi-Purpose Youth and Recreation 
Centres 
There is a strong desire for youth-specific spaces like 
youth centres, gym/sports centres, study spaces and 
affordable gyms for teenagers. 
 
3. Organise Regular Community Events and 
Entertainment 
Young people are asking for more live music venues, 
small concerts, group/social recreation, and places to 
hang out. 24 hour toilet facilities and better lighting in 
public spaces were also mentioned.

conjunction with the Department of Transport with funding being provided 
by the Climate Action Fund.
